extracted.intended_audience: readers of Coleridge's biography; literary critics, students of poetry and literary history
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-introduction guidance on how to judge an author's originality, borrowing, memory/quotation accuracy, metrical/translation quality, moral character, and the relation of literature to religious opinion. Uses Coleridge as the exemplar but states general principles for literary judgment and editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of borrowed material
rubrics_metrics.description: Had the author superintended the edition, ... he would, perhaps, have made reference to Schiller and Stolberg in these instances, as he had done in others; if he neglected to do so, it could not have been in expectation of keeping to himself what he had borrowed in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing or republishing material that draws on other authors, the editor/author ought to make precise references to those sources. Failure to state obligations is blameworthy; editions should state explicitly what is borrowed (example: references to Schiller and Stolberg).

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs derivation in assessing poetic merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Is not such glory the substance, of poetic merit? How much of admiration we not unsubstantialize, if the reproduction of... with additions and improvements, is to be made...?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce merit solely to strict novelty: a work that reproduces another with meaningful additions or improvements can possess substantial poetic merit. Evaluate both derivation and the value of the transformations/augmentations rather than dismissing all borrowing as merely 'shadow'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical and linguistic excellence in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: To my ear... the light dactylic flow of the latter... is still more exquisite in the English than in the original; the pentameter... the spondee which commences the latter is an advantage... the line is rather the more liquid of the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging translations, attend to metrical effect and language: a translation can improve upon or alter metrical qualities in ways that make it more (or less) effective in the target language. Compare original and translated metres (pentameter, hexameter, elegiac distich) and judge by their aural and rhetorical effects, not only by literal fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of quotation and factual citation
rubrics_metrics.description: At all times his incorrectness of quotation and the relation of particular circumstances, was extreme... It is the duty of any man, who hath such a peculiarity, to watch over it and endeavor to remedy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars and writers have a duty to ensure accuracy in quotation and factual detail. Persistent incorrect quotation is a serious fault; where a writer knows his memory is fallible, he must take steps to verify and correct quotations and particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish unconscious appropriation from deliberate fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: My Father's forgetfulness was not appropriation... He did not publish this Lecture himself. Whenever it is re‑published, what it contains of Schelling's will be stated precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing alleged borrowing, consider intent and context. Intellectual temperament and memory errors can lead to unconscious appropriation; editors should state precisely what is derived from others and avoid accusing authors of deliberate theft when evidence points to unconscious adoption or oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize conduct by intellectual temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Men of 'peculiar intellectual conformation'... points in conduct, which in persons of ordinary faculties... could only result from conscious wilful departure from the rule of right, may in their case have a different origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging an author's lapses (errors of citation, inconsistency in conduct), account for psychological and temperamental factors. Peculiar intellectual gifts may be accompanied by corresponding defects; these should affect how blame and responsibility are assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assess ideas solely by the author's personal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions be tried on their own merits, and if this is best the inquirer’s purpose, ... let him disdain an argument in their favor, out of themselves, from doubtful considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments and opinions on their intrinsic merits rather than by attempting to infer their truth from the author's life or alleged personal faults. Tracing origins of beliefs in a person's biography is a risky and often misleading way to judge doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hominem attempts to discredit thought
rubrics_metrics.description: For one man who reads and deeply examine any portion of the opinions... there are hundreds ... who are glad to come at them obliquely, by lowering the personal character and thereby weakening his authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of criticisms that target personal character to undermine intellectual positions (examples drawn from attempts to discredit Luther or Coleridge). Such methods are circuitous and uncertain; prefer direct engagement with the arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly precision in editorial attributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it is re-published, what it contains of Schelling's will be stated precisely. Would that an equal restitution could be made in all quarters of all that has been borrowed...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors preparing posthumous or collected editions should precisely indicate what portions are borrowed, quoted, or translated. Clear attributions and restitution of sources are required scholarly practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of authorship versus commercial compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: If he had calculated at all he would have... but to calculate was not in his nature. If he ever deceived it was when he was himself deceived first... literature can scarcely be made the means of living, without being debased; but he himself failed in the art of living, because he would not thus debase it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should resist sacrificing higher literary or intellectual aims for immediate popular success or commercial gain. Compromising literary integrity to adapt to the 'ways of newspapers' or vulgar periodicals debases literature and can distort an author's religious/scholarly sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of literary engagement with tradition and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: He aimed... to bring ancient religious metaphysics and neglected arguments into current use... a very different process from that of a true reformer, which, instead of raising up the dead body of ancient doctrine, calls forth the life and substance that belong to it, clothing it in newer and more spiritual body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviving or using older doctrines or literary material, aim to reinvigorate and make them living and relevant rather than merely recycling obsolete argument. The critic/author’s task is to elicit the living substance in tradition and express it afresh to contemporary minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance words and deeds in judging affections and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Kind words are not to be contrasted with good deeds, except where they are substitutes for them... those kindly feelings which... often overflowed in words, were just as ready to shape themselves into deeds, as far as the heart was concerned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a writer's moral character by both expressed sentiments and demonstrated actions. Overflowing words can be genuine and often correspond to deeds; do not hastily dismiss warm expression as mere verbalism without investigating concrete conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate evidentiary standards for religious or metaphysical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The common argument in behalf of those who are commonly so called rests upon historical testimony and outward evidence; why should the profession of literature render men less able to estimate proof of this nature?... It is not contended that my Father was, during his whole life, in the position for appreciating Catholicity... but he never was so circumstanced as to be precluded from drawing nigh to any true system existing in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging religious doctrines, be clear about the types of evidence being used (historical testimony, inward argument, experiential habit). Different intellectual pursuits (literature, reflection) shape how one approaches such evidence, but one should not assume incapacity merely from profession.
